coverage.method: Complete page-by-page extracted text read; rendered pages separately listed where inspected.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Counter-revolution: origins and heterogeneous boundaries
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Doyle dates counter-revolution proper to the challenge to national sovereignty in June 1789. The Royal Session programme retained orders, privileges and feudal rights while conceding reforms. Later defectors were not welcomed uniformly.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: counter-revolution; national sovereignty; Royal Session of 23 June; restoration programmes
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not project organized counter-revolution before the Revolution or treat it as a single stable doctrine.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Emigration: successive motives, geography and leadership
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Artois and courtiers left after July; rural violence, constitutional disappointment, abolition of nobility, army mutiny, suppressed offices and religious reform widened the stream. Turin coordination, Calonne’s wealth and expertise, and weak foreign backing matter separately.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: émigrés; Artois; Calonne; Turin; noble/officer/clerical emigration
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Check causal phases and groups rather than only a collective label or a list of exile destinations.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Domestic royal rescue schemes and constitutional monarchy
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Favras’s failed rescue conspiracy differs from Mirabeau’s paid advice and plans. Doyle expressly denies that Mirabeau was a counter-revolutionary, although their practical schemes resembled each other. Louis XVI’s refusal to act weakened these projects.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Favras conspiracy; Mirabeau and royal advice; Louis XVI and escape plans
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep ideological distinction and agency. Do not infer all royal rescue planning was émigré counter-revolution.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Southern sectarian resistance: Nîmes, Jalès and royalist organization
findings.source_grounded_analysis: The Nîmes violence mobilized inherited Catholic-Protestant antagonism sharpened by revolutionary reform. Froment linked it to Artois; Catholic martyrdom deepened royalism. Jalès camps and the premature 1792 rising did not demonstrate a reliable nationwide army.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Nîmes bagarre; Froment; Jalès camps; Catholic-Protestant conflict; Midi royalism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Retain religious, local and organizing distinctions plus the failure of promises of foreign support.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Failed Lyonnais projects and counter-revolution within the Assembly
findings.source_grounded_analysis: A proposed Lyon-based royal rescue and southern rising collapsed through non-cooperation and exposure. Cazalès and Maury later cultivated extreme measures in hope of discrediting the new order; this differs from straightforward radical conviction.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Lyons royalist plots; Cazalès; Maury; obstruction in Constituent Assembly
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Represent tactical extremism as tactical, and avoid merging the 1790 plot with the 1793 revolt.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Varennes and militarization of emigration
findings.source_grounded_analysis: The failed flight made royal coercion plausible to foreign rulers, increased officer emigration, and accelerated military organization at Koblenz. Pillnitz and subsidies raised hopes, but forces were auxiliaries and ultimately lacked resources and secure bases.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Varennes consequences; émigré armies; Koblenz; Black Legion; Pillnitz; foreign subsidies
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Check relations: Varennes accelerated militarization; Pillnitz encouraged expectations rather than guaranteed intervention.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Bourbon restoration manifestos and refusal of revolutionary gains
findings.source_grounded_analysis: The princes’ September 1791 letter denied constitutional legitimacy; the 1793 regency proclamation and Verona in 1795 maintained an intransigent programme. The programme antagonized constitutional royalists and potential allies.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Provence/Louis XVIII; Declaration of Verona; émigré manifestos; constitutional royalism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Retain phases and refusal of gains; verify date language against noted source inconsistency.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Émigré society: exclusiveness alongside sacrifice
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Exile courts reproduced status distinctions and hostility to latecomers, burdening hosts. Doyle also recognizes genuine risk, devotion and willingness of former officers to serve in ranks, exemplified by Chateaubriand.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: émigré social hierarchy; noble exclusiveness; exile experience; Chateaubriand
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Avoid a wholly contemptuous or uniformly self-interested stance; the qualification is substantive.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Anti-revolution transformed into counter-revolution
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Disappointment alone did not entail Bourbon restoration. Clerical-oath enforcement, repression and central intrusion helped turn hostility into organized Church-and-king resistance; western conscription was the trigger rather than the complete cause.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: anti-revolution; popular counter-revolution; refractory clergy; conscription; local autonomy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: A broad counter-revolution record must preserve distinct motives, chronology and the limited geographic scope of mass royalism.

findings.subject_or_distinction: La Rouërie and Breton association
findings.source_grounded_analysis: The Breton association combined provincial attachment, clerical resistance, arms acquisition and links with the princes. Its organizers struggled to keep contacts at home instead of emigrating and lacked a clear operational plan.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: La Rouërie; Breton association; Brittany royalism
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Require usable institutional/person routes and avoid conflating the association with later chouan command claims.

findings.subject_or_distinction: 1792 invasion, Valmy and disintegration of émigré forces
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Émigré optimism and Brunswick threats failed to draw popular support. Defeat and retreat broke up most forces, leaving Condé’s units exceptional. War intended to restore royal power instead helped destroy it.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Valmy and émigrés; Brunswick Manifesto; Condé’s army; émigré diaspora
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve the causal irony as Doyle’s argument; do not imply émigrés fought at the Valmy cannonade.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Foreign powers: conditional support and competing interests
findings.source_grounded_analysis: British sea power created possibilities for western royalists, but Britain prioritized limiting French power, colonies and strategic footholds. Other powers also resisted permanent commitment to Bourbon objectives. Recognition of Provence was very limited.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Britain and counter-revolution; foreign intervention; Bourbon recognition; West Indies strategy
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not encode foreign war as an unqualified campaign to restore the old regime or all émigré complaints as narrator-endorsed fact.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Western peasant grievances and Catholic royal armies
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Light seigneurial burdens, tenancy, rents after tithe abolition, hostility to imposed priests, taxes and intrusive government explain why western peasants saw fewer gains and higher burdens. Vendéans coalesced; Breton chouans remained dispersed.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Vendée causes; Brittany; tithe abolition and tenants; conscription resistance; Catholic and royal army
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Keep economic/religious/local explanations together without reducing the revolt to clergy or nobles.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Federalism and limited royalism
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Opposition to Convention rule did not normally seek old-regime restoration. Royalists exploited Caen and Lyons, while Toulon called the British and declared monarchy chiefly from fear; Hood offered the 1791 constitution, not the princes’ programme.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Federalist revolt and royalism; Toulon; Hood; constitution of 1791
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Require careful scope: involvement is not identity; distinguish Toulon’s conditional declaration from western popular royalism.

findings.subject_or_distinction: British intervention logistics and representation of insurgents
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Granville failed to meet Moira’s force; future British help required a port. Puisaye exaggerated both chouan strength and his authority; the guerrillas were disruptive but unable to hold a port. British strategic isolation made his proposal attractive.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Granville expedition; Moira; Puisaye; chouannerie; Channel Islands; amphibious intervention
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve claims as claims and the gap between guerrilla effectiveness and conventional military capability.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Royalist constitutionalists, propaganda and intelligence
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Mallet du Pan argued revolutionary gains required guarantees and supplied intelligence; d’Antraigues’s rival network altered reports to support uncompromising restoration. Pures and constitutionals also differed internally.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Mallet du Pan; d’Antraigues; royalist intelligence; pures; constitutionals
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not merge intelligence networks, treat each as reliable, or flatten constitutionalists into one constitutional design.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Hoche’s pacification and tactical insurgent truces
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Religious toleration, disciplined republican forces, military pressure and supply shortages made 1795 truces possible. Some leaders signed tactically, and not all chouans accepted La Mabilais. Later saturation and executions reduced revolt to precarious peace.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Hoche; La Mabilais; Vendée pacification; Charette; Stofflet; religious toleration
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Distinguish the leaders’ deceptive professions from declining popular grievances; preserve precariousness of peace.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Quiberon expedition and Yeu failure
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Poor discipline and unclear command prevented expansion from Quiberon; Hoche’s counterattack captured many and led to executions under émigré laws. Artois arrived too late and the Yeu venture failed to link with Charette. Competing factions blamed Puisaye and Britain.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Quiberon expedition; émigré executions; Île d’Yeu; Artois; Charette; Cadoudal
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Separate military outcome, penal aftermath, failed follow-up and factional interpretation. Retain source date as uncertain if needing comparison.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Condé, Pichegru and d’Antraigues after 1795
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Rhine schemes envisaged linkage with Lyonnais royalists, but recruitment of Pichegru paralysed action. Bonaparte’s capture of d’Antraigues revealed damaging intelligence in an explicitly murky episode. Louis XVIII was expelled from successive refuges.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: Pichegru and royalist intrigue; Condé; d’Antraigues capture; Louis XVIII exile
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Do not overstate clarity of the intelligence affair; distinguish planned military coordination from realized action.

findings.subject_or_distinction: Why armed counter-revolution failed; turn toward elections
findings.source_grounded_analysis: Factional conflict, incompatible foreign aims, local peasant horizons and republican military power defeated armed restoration by Leoben. Doyle doubts even a royal landing would have induced a western march to Paris. Constitutional monarchy could still gain through elections.
findings.reader_routes_to_check: failure of counter-revolution; localism; royalist electoral prospects; Leoben
findings.eventual_draft_checks: Preserve counterfactual uncertainty and separate defeat of armed restoration from disappearance of royalism.

uncertainties.issue: Page 303 visibly prints 13 June programme; pages 297 and 310 identify 23 June. Preserve as source inconsistency rather than silently normalizing all evidence.

The source visibly dates Hoche’s Quiberon attack to 3 July and recapture within a week. No external chronology has been consulted; any draft using another date requires explicit source reconciliation.
